## Psalm 40 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1: "I waited patiently for the LORD; He inclined to me and heard my cry."

- **Traditional reading:** The Hebrew is "waiting I waited" — an intensive doubling that stresses diligent, persevering patience. David had practiced waiting in Psalms 37–39; here the answer arrives. Spurgeon applies this to Christ: "Patient waiting upon God was a special characteristic of our Lord Jesus … all through his agony … no word of murmuring came from God's patient Lamb." Matthew Henry sees it speaking both of David's deliverance and of Christ's endurance in Gethsemane and the cross. Guzik (Enduring Word) notes that the word "inclined" conveys God bending down to David, removing perceived distance.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-40/
  - https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps040.php
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/40.htm
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/40.htm

### v. 2: "He lifted me up from the pit of despair, out of the miry clay; He set my feet upon a rock, and made my footsteps firm."

- **Traditional reading:** The "horrible pit" (also rendered "pit of destruction/noisy pit") and "miry clay" picture despair, danger, and having no foothold. Spurgeon reads this Christologically: "When our Lord bore in his own person the terrible curse which was due to sin, he was so cast down as to be like a prisoner in a deep, dark, fearful dungeon." The "rock" represents security; the "established goings" point to Christ's completed work and resurrection. The Pulpit Commentary treats the imagery as spiritual deliverance: the penitent lifted from the mire of sin and guilt and set on the Rock of Ages. Matthew Henry calls Christ himself "the Rock on which a poor soul can alone stand fast."
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-40/
  - https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps040.php
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/40.htm
  - https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/40.htm (Pulpit Homiletics)

### v. 3: "He put a new song in my mouth, a hymn of praise to our God. Many will see and fear and put their trust in the LORD."

- **Traditional reading:** The "new song" is praise for a fresh act of deliverance — not the old creation-song but the song of redeeming grace (Pulpit). Spurgeon calls it the song that Jesus now leads among the redeemed: "Justice magnified and grace victorious; hell subdued and heaven glorified … what a theme for a hymn!" Gill sees the new song as sung by Christ in the great congregation upon his resurrection and ascension, joined by all his people (Rev 5:9). Guzik says God Himself inspires the song; it is right for the creature to praise the Creator and the delivered to praise the Deliverer. The testimony of deliverance causes "many" to fear the Lord and trust in Him.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-40/
  - https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps040.php
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/40.htm
  - https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/40.htm

### v. 4: "Blessed is the man who has made the LORD his trust, who has not turned to the proud, nor to those who lapse into falsehood."

- **Traditional reading:** This is the first "beatitude" flowing from David's experience. Spurgeon: "A man may be as poor as Lazarus, as hated as Mordecai, as sick as Hezekiah, as lonely as Elijah, but while his hand of faith can keep its hold on God, none of his outward afflictions can prevent his being numbered among the blessed." Trusting God and refusing to honor the proud or follow lies are connected — true faith shapes moral discernment. Guzik notes the proud are called by the same term that became a nickname for Egypt ("Rahab," the empty blusterer; Isaiah 30:7).
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-40/
  - https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps040.php
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/40.htm

### v. 5: "Many, O LORD my God, are the wonders You have done, and the plans You have for us — none can compare to You — if I proclaim and declare them, they are more than I can count."

- **Traditional reading:** God's "wonderful works" are seen in creation, providence, and redemption. His "thoughts" (or plans) toward His people are numberless and gracious. Spurgeon marvels: "When I think, it is a poor, little, weak, empty head that is thinking; but when God thinks, the gigantic mind which framed the universe is thinking upon me." Gill notes these thoughts refer to God's eternal decrees and purposes. Kidner (cited by Guzik) sees the past as "full of His miracles" and the future "full of His plans."
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-40/
  - https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps040.php
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/40.htm

### v. 6: "Sacrifice and offering You did not desire, but my ears You have opened. Burnt offerings and sin offerings You did not require."

- **Traditional reading — Bond-Servant imagery:** The phrase "my ears You have opened" (literally "ears You have dug/bored") is widely understood as an allusion to the pierced ear of the willing bond-servant in Exodus 21:5–6. David Guzik: a servant who loved his master would have his ear pierced with an awl as a sign of lifelong, voluntary service. David's "two ears" (rather than one) express total surrender. Spurgeon agrees: "Jesus irrevocably gave himself up to be the servant of servants." Gill and JFB see the primary sense as obedience — ears opened to hear and do God's will.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-40/
  - https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps040.php
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/40.htm
  - https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/psalms/40.htm

- **Septuagint variation in Hebrews 10:5:** The LXX renders "a body You have prepared for Me" rather than "my ears You have opened." Spurgeon accepts this as "an instance of various readings equally inspired" under apostolic authority. Gill explains: the body is implied — without a body, ears could not be opened. The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary affirms that the "opened ear symbolizes obedience" while the "special body" prepared for Jesus was the means by which He bore our sins.
  - https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps040.php
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/40.htm
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/psalms-40.html

- **Barnes' alternative view (non-bondservant):** Albert Barnes (cited on biblehub.com) argues against the Exodus 21 allusion, seeing "digged" as meaning "opened" or "excavated" — i.e., made able to hear, with no reference to piercing. He finds the Septuagint rendering difficult to explain. (Barnes' Notes at biblehub.com, v. 6 page.)
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/40-6.htm

### v. 7: "Then I said, 'Here I am, I have come — it is written about me in the scroll:'"

- **Traditional reading:** Spurgeon calls this the moment "when it was clearly seen that man's misery could not be remedied by sacrifices and offerings … the Lord Jesus, in propria persona, intervened." "Lo, I come" is the highlight of the Psalm (Coffman). The "scroll of the book" refers to the eternal decree, the covenant of redemption, and the Old Testament Scriptures that foretold Christ. Gill specifies the "volume of the book" as the five books of Moses (the only completed canon when David wrote), particularly Genesis 3:15. Matthew Henry: "In the close rolls of the Divine decrees and counsel, the covenant of redemption was recorded. Also, in all the volumes of the Old Testament something was written of him."
  - https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps040.php
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/40.htm
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/40.htm
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-40.html

### v. 8: "I delight to do Your will, O my God; Your law is within my heart."

- **Traditional reading:** Only Christ perfectly fulfilled this. Spurgeon: "Jesus not only did the Father's will, but found a delight therein … even in Gethsemane itself he chose the Father's will, and set aside his own." The law was not an external burden but internalized — "within my heart." This obedience is "our righteousness" (Spurgeon). Guzik notes Jesus said doing God's will was as necessary and delightful as food (John 4:34). Gill sees the "law within my heart" as referring both to the whole moral law and to the specific command to offer Himself as a sacrifice.
  - https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps040.php
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-40/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/40.htm

### v. 9: "I proclaim righteousness in the great assembly; behold, I do not seal my lips, as You, O LORD, do know."

- **Traditional reading:** The Hebrew verb here means "to proclaim good news" (Septuagint: "evangelizavi"). David speaks of publicly declaring God's righteousness. But the ultimate speaker is Christ: Spurgeon calls Jesus "the Prince of open-air preachers, the Great Itinerant, the President of the College of all preachers of the gospel." Matthew Henry: "Whoever undertook to preach the gospel of Christ would be under great temptation to conceal it; but Christ … [was] carried on in it."
  - https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps040.php
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-40/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/40.htm

### v. 10: "I have not covered up Your righteousness in my heart; I have declared Your faithfulness and salvation; I have not concealed Your loving devotion and faithfulness from the great assembly."

- **Traditional reading:** The four attributes declared — righteousness, faithfulness, salvation, lovingkindness/truth — summarize the gospel message. Spurgeon: "God, faithful to his own character, law and threatenings, and yet saving sinners, is a peculiar revelation of the gospel." Jesus "kept back nothing which would be profitable" (Spurgeon). Gill explains "faithfulness" as God fulfilling His covenant promises in Christ, and "salvation" as the great gospel doctrine.
  - https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps040.php
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/40.htm

### v. 11: "O LORD, do not withhold Your mercy from me; Your loving devotion and faithfulness will always guard me."

- **Traditional reading:** The shift from praise to petition is sudden. David (and Christ) will not presume on future mercy. Spurgeon reads this as Christ's prayer before the cross: "Alas! these were to be for awhile withheld from our Lord while on the accursed tree … the coming of the angel to strengthen him was a clear answer." Guzik sees this as a prayer Jesus might have prayed on the cross. Some commentators (Gill, Gejerus) read this not as petition but as declaration of faith: "Thou wilt not withhold; Thy lovingkindness shall continually preserve me."
  - https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps040.php
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-40/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/40.htm

### v. 12: "For evils without number surround me; my sins have overtaken me, so that I cannot see. They are more than the hairs of my head, and my heart has failed within me."

- **Traditional reading — the crux of Christological interpretation:** David speaks of his own sins. But applied to Christ, these are "my iniquities" by imputation — sins He bore as Substitute, not sins He committed. Spurgeon: "He had no sin, but sins were laid on him, and he took them as if they were his … 'He was made sin for us.'" John Trapp (cited by Spurgeon and Guzik): Christ is "Maximus peccatorum, the greatest of sinners by imputation, 2 Corinthians 5:21." Matthew Henry: "The sight and sense of our sins in their own colours, must distract us, if we have not at the same time some sight of a Saviour." The phrase "cannot see" suggests being so overwhelmed by sin-bearing that looking up to the Father's face was impossible.
  - https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps040.php
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-40/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/40.htm
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/40.htm

### v. 13: "Be pleased, O LORD, to deliver me; hurry, O LORD, to help me."

- **Traditional reading:** David asks not just for deliverance but for God to *take pleasure* in delivering him — a bold and skillful request based on confidence in God's character. Guzik applies the pattern: "Be pleased, O LORD, to forgive … to correct … to provide …" Gill sees this fulfilled in Christ's resurrection: deliverance from death and the grave, done because "God's well pleasedness" rested on Him (Psalm 22:8). The urgency — "make haste" — is honest and human.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-40/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/40.htm
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/40.htm

### v. 14: "May those who seek my life be ashamed and confounded; may those who wish me harm be repelled and humiliated."

- **Traditional reading:** This imprecatory prayer is for the dishonoring of David's enemies according to divine justice. Guzik cites VanGemeren: "The psalmist prays for his enemies' fall … in accordance with the principles of justice and with the promise of God to curse those who cursed his own." Spurgeon applies it Christologically — those who persecuted Jesus will be confounded.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-40/
  - https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps040.php

### v. 15: "May those who say to me, 'Aha, aha!' be appalled at their own shame."

- **Traditional reading:** The taunt "Aha! Aha!" is the gloating cry of enemies. Adam Clarke (cited by Guzik) warns: "O ungodly reader … beware of persecuting Christ and his people, for God will surely avenge his own elect. Your 'ahas' will cost you dear."
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-40/

### v. 16: "May all who seek You rejoice and be glad in You; may those who love Your salvation always say, 'The LORD be magnified!'"

- **Traditional reading:** David contrasts the fate of enemies with the joy of God's people. To "magnify" the LORD is to make Him larger in one's perception — not making God bigger, but perceiving Him as greater. Goodwin (cited by Spurgeon) notes that the godly love salvation "not as his own only, but as God's … 'that love thy salvation.'"
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-40/
  - https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps040.php

### v. 17: "But I am poor and needy; may the Lord think of me. You are my helper and deliverer; O my God, do not delay."

- **Traditional reading:** The psalm's closing paradox: "I am poor and needy; yet the LORD thinks upon me." Guzik: "security in God's care of us doesn't erase our real need, but transforms how we face it." Spurgeon: "He cries, 'I am poor and needy.' His joy is found in Another." The final plea "do not delay" circles back to the opening theme of waiting — David has learned patience through experience, yet still asks with raw honesty. Matthew Henry: "The prayer of faith can unlock his fulness, which is adapted to all their wants. The promises are sure, the moment of fulfilment hastens forward."
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-40/
  - https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps040.php
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/40.htm

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### The Christological reading of vv. 6–8 (and v. 12)

- **Reformed/Baptist (Spurgeon, Gill, JFB):** These teachers hold that vv. 6–10 are *primarily or exclusively* about Christ, not David. Spurgeon: "Even if the New Testament were not so express upon it, we should have concluded that David spoke of our Lord … the apostle in Heb 10:5-9 puts all conjecture out of court." Gill says the Psalm title ("for David, a psalm") can be rendered "a psalm concerning David" — meaning David's antitype, the Messiah.
  - https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps040.php
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/40.htm
  - https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/psalms/40.htm

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word — David Guzik):** Guzik holds a both/and reading: David's surrender foreshadows Christ's ultimate surrender, but the passage *also* has a real application to David's own life. "David's surrender to God was wonderful … Yet he only foreshadowed the ultimate submission … by the Messiah." The bond-servant imagery is applied to David's actual heart-attitude toward God before it is applied to Jesus.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-40/

- **Anglican (Ellicott):** Ellicott is notably cautious about Davidic authorship: it is "rejected, even by such critics as Delitzsch," and the psalm may have been written after the discovery of the Book of the Law in Josiah's reign by a Deuteronomist. He notes the composite nature of the psalm (vv. 1–10 praise, vv. 11–17 prayer, with vv. 13–17 reappearing as Psalm 70). Yet the prophetic spirit of the singer "exalts spiritual above merely formal religion."
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/40.htm

- **Methodist/Wesleyan/Holiness — Pulpit Homiletics:** The Pulpit Commentary treats the psalm as David's own and the deliverance as primarily spiritual — from "the mire of sin and guilt." The application to Christ is noted but the emphasis is on the believer's experience of grace producing (1) surrender of will and (2) public proclamation. The doctrine that obedience is better than sacrifice is traced through 1 Samuel 15:22, Psalm 51:16, Isaiah 1:11, Jeremiah 7:21, Hosea 6:6, and Micah 6:1–8 — showing it is no late development.
  - https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/40.htm

### The "body prepared" vs. "ears opened" question (v. 6)

- **Those who see the LXX as inspired/authoritative (Spurgeon, many Reformed):** Spurgeon calls the Septuagint reading "a body You have prepared for Me" an instance of "various readings equally inspired" because apostolic authority (Hebrews 10:5) sanctioned it.
  - https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps040.php

- **Those who see the Hebrew as primary (Barnes, many conservative Baptists):** Barnes argues the original "ears You have dug" means opened to hear and obey, with no reference to the bond-servant ceremony. The LXX is a paraphrase whose origin "it is not easy to imagine." He acknowledges the difficulty this creates for the Hebrews 10:5 quotation.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/40-6.htm

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship (Ellicott / Cambridge Bible)

- **Composite Psalm theory:** Ellicott notes that the "burst of praise (Psalm 40:1-10), followed by plaintive prayer (Psalm 40:11 onwards), is so peculiar … as to lead … to the conjecture of a composite poem." The fact that vv. 13–17 appear again as Psalm 70 supports this. Davidic authorship is rejected by critics such as Delitzsch; the psalm may date from Josiah's reign, after the discovery of the Book of the Law.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/40.htm

- **Cambridge Bible:** Notes that vv. 6ff gain fresh force when connected with 1 Samuel 15:22 (Saul's rejection). The self-devotion of the king after God's own heart is "the exact opposite of the self-will which was the ground of Saul's rejection."
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/psalms/40.htm

### Jewish Interpretation (noted by Gill)

- Jarchi (Rashi) interpreted the psalm of the Israelites and their deliverance and song at the Red Sea. Kimchi saw the subject as the same as the two preceding psalms. R. Obadiah thought David composed it when recovered from leprosy. Theodoret noted some applied it to Jeremiah in the dungeon or Daniel in the den. But Gill insists it is "not concerning David himself, but concerning his antitype and son."
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/40.htm
